title: Green spaces in cities: more, better and more connected?
content:
Abstract
Urban green spaces provide a broad range of benefits to society, making them an important element of natural capital accounting. Natural capital accounting in cities aims to capture not only the quantity of green spaces, but also their quality and spatial configuration, as these all influence the benefits we receive from them. So far, few studies have explored the links between these three characteristics or “dimensions” of natural capital, even though it has implications for both monitoring efforts and management. To address this knowledge gap, we assess the correlation structure between different indicators for the quantity, quality and spatial configuration of green spaces, using Greater London as a case study. All considered indicators show significant association with each other, thus containing some redundancy for coarse-grained monitoring exercises. However, the strength of correlation varies between different indicators, with spatial configuration and quantity generally displaying strong positive correlation, highlighting that each dimension still has its own independent value for management decisions. Species richness, an indicator of quality, shows the weakest correlation with the quantity of green area; this implies that to create highly biodiverse areas in urban settings, simply extending the area of habitat may not be enough and more targeted management is likely to be necessary.
